rationale: B wins because it has cleaner strategic judgment: four real lanes, no filler, and one angle A missed entirely: "Why Ramp is giving away an agent that finds six figures in savings." A is smart, but it starts decorating around the facts with "Spend visibility alone didn't save these 200 companies" and then admits the premise is only "presumably" true. That is not fatal, but it is the kind of shaky board a reporter steps on once and never trusts again.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors to cancel the software nobody's using" overstates the mechanics. The update says the agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves, not that the agent sends them.
"The average company wastes $342,000 a year" turns a 200-company beta average into a market-wide claim. That is how you get a data reporter to ask for methodology before they even says hello.

"As Ramp customers, this beta group presumably already had spend visibility" is an unsupported premise carrying an entire contrarian angle. If the beta group was not existing Ramp spend-visibility users, the angle collapses.
"An AI agent is now doing part of the procurement analyst's job" reaches toward labor displacement without labor evidence. A correctly cautious proof note does not fully save an over-eager headline.
gaps_in_B: "Companies are paying an average of $342,000 a year for software nobody is using" still over-generalizes the beta. The update supports "Ramp beta companies" and "savings found," not all companies or banked savings.

"software vendors' renewal playbooks (auto-renewals, quiet seat expansion)" sneaks in "quiet seat expansion," which is not in the update. Auto-renewals and unused seats are enough; don't gild the invoice.

"monetization deferred to a future enterprise tier" is a plausible strategy read, but the update only says an enterprise tier with custom approval workflows is coming later this year. Pricing and monetization need an on-record answer before that line carries weight.
